newsitem.title: USA: US, Japan, Canadian currencies defy trade balances.
newsitem.headline: US, Japan, Canadian currencies defy trade balances.

text.p: The release of ostensibly dollar-negative trade reports from the U.S., Canada and Japan on Thursday, did little to dent the enthusiasm of dollar bulls who seem more pre-occupied with strong U.S. economic fundamentals.
"I think the trade numbers should not stand in the way of a further dollar advance," said Chris Widness, international economist at Chase Securities Inc.

Real interest rate differentials are dictating the direction of these currencies, not trade balances, experts said. Greater prospects for higher U.S. interest rates versus those in Canada and Japan translate into a higher dollar.

The dollar hit a 56-month high against the yen last week while the Canadian dollar reached a two-year low against the dollar on Thursday despite growing trade surpluses in Canada and Japan and a worrying U.S. trade deficit.

"Were we expecting an epiphany in the currency markets on Thursday? Not really," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics, referring to foreign exchange market reaction to the trade figures.
"However, we do expect the figures will undermine some of the unbridled dollar bullishness we are hearing about," he added.

Economists were quick to note that even sharp, major reversals in trade accounts typically take years to flow through into the currency markets and vice versa -- an economic principal known as the J-curve effect.

Also, Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc, said the popular "yen carry trade", where investors borrow in low-cost yen to invest in U.S. assets and reap the income differential, would not show up in goods and services trade balances, but greatly alters currency supply and demand.
Early morning U.S. foreign exchange trade played out the conflict between dollar-adverse trade reports and supportive economic fundamentals.

Dealers tried to push the dollar lower immediately following a less-than-expected fall in the U.S. February trade deficit to $11.59 billion from January's near decade-high $12.67 shortfall, but met with staunch resistance.

"The markets tried to sell-off on the number, but the dollar can't really go down and it seems like a lot of people are getting their heads handed to them," said Ron Leven, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan.
The dollar was mixed in mid-afternoon trade, posting small gains against the yen and losing ground versus the mark.

The Canadian dollar had sunk to it lowest level against the U.S. dollar since April of 1995 in afternoon trade after news its merchandise trade surplus widened in February to C$2.19 billion from a revised C$1.97 billion.

Overnight, the yen briefly strengthened against the dollar on news Japan's overall customs-cleared trade surplus narrowed 27 percent in the year to March and its politically sensitive bilateral trade surplus with the United States rose 11.2 percent to 379.83 billion yen.
However, the gains were short-lived.

Aiding the dollar was a healthy 4.0 percent rise in U.S. exports, which refuted arguments that recent strength in the greenback was hurting U.S. competitiveness abroad by making U.S. goods relatively more expensive.
"I don't think the dollar is what's driving the (trade) numbers," said Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich on Thursday.
Rather, economists pinned the above-forecast trade gap on strong demand pushing import growth up a surprising 2.1 percent.

"This is a symptom of our success. If you have an economy which is growing close to 5.0 percent in real terms in the first quarter, you're going to get a huge surge in imports," said David Kelly, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics.
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk 212-859-1677))
